827.title: Where you go
827.hook: Ruth to Naomi: where you go I will go
827.howItsDone: Ruth's words to Naomi are read at some weddings and conversion ceremonies, and in Jewish communities the book of Ruth is read at the festival of Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the command to love the stranger. Your line was you were strangers. Did a newcomer get a welcome from you? Today, a stranger who chose to stay. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

Three widows are standing on a road out of Moab. Naomi, the older one, has buried her husband and both her sons. Her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, have buried their husbands too. Naomi is heading home to Bethlehem, and she stops and tells the young women to turn around: "Go, return each to her mother's house." She has nothing left to give them. They cry. Orpah kisses her and goes. Ruth doesn't move. The King James puts it in a handful of words: "Ruth clave unto her." Today: what Ruth said next, and what it costs to stay.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH KISSES HER AND GOES.` → `RUTH DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: Start with the one who leaves, because the story is kind to her. Naomi asked both women to go, and she blessed them on the way: "the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me." Orpah does what she was asked. The text never scolds her. Going home was sensible, and it was allowed. That's what makes Ruth's choice stand out. She had an honorable way out, and she didn't take it. Look at the verb. "Ruth clave unto her." It's the same English verb the King James uses in Genesis for a man who will "cleave unto his wife." Clinging, holding on. Then she speaks. Earlier this year we heard her opening words, whither thou goest. Today, the line that follows them, which goes further: "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried." Ruth isn't promising a trip. She's promising a whole life, and a grave, in a country where she will be the foreigner. Yesterday's stranger, seen from the other side. Notice what kind of promise it is. She doesn't talk about how she feels. She names a direction: where you go. And the story shows what that looks like on an ordinary day. In Bethlehem, Ruth goes out to glean, gathering leftover barley behind the reapers in someone else's field so the two of them can eat. Later the field's owner, Boaz, says something curious to her: "thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning." The Hebrew word behind kindness there is chesed, the steady, loyal love we met at the start of this block. Some readers take that sentence as the book's quiet center: love that keeps going after the moment when leaving would have been fine.
screen: `ORPAH GOES, AND NO ONE BLAMES HER.` · `RUTH CLAVE UNTO HER.` · `WHERE THOU DIEST, WILL I DIE.` · `KINDNESS IN THE LATTER END.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is in a hard stretch right now, someone it would be easy, and even reasonable, to drift away from. Breathe, and let their face settle in front of you. Picture walking beside them for one more mile. You're not fixing anything. You're just staying. Then ask, quietly: what would staying look like this week? A call. A ride. An hour on their couch. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. Let the rest be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Where you go. Ruth's answer on the road: loyalty with a direction, staying when going home would have been allowed. Today's word.
Your line: where you go. Today, take one step toward the person you chose, a message or a visit, and stay a little longer than you planned. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: David and Jonathan
828.hook: David mourns Jonathan's love as wonderful
828.howItsDone: Readers of the Hebrew Bible point to David and Jonathan as a picture of loyal friendship, and some keep up old friendships with letters, calls or visits on anniversaries and holidays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth on the road. Your line was where you go. Did you take a step toward the person you chose to stay with? Today, another kind of loyalty: two friends. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

"Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women." A warrior sings that over a dead friend. The news has just reached David: King Saul and his son Jonathan have fallen in battle on Mount Gilboa. Saul has hunted David. Jonathan was Saul's son, the heir to the throne David would one day take. By the usual rules of politics, they should have been rivals. Instead, near the end of David's lament come Jonathan's name and that line. Today: how that friendship began, what it cost, and what David did with it after the funeral.
screen: `THY LOVE TO ME WAS WONDERFUL.` → `THE KING'S SON, AND HIS RIVAL.` → `BEGINNING, COST, AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: It begins with a sentence that doesn't sound like politics at all. After David's victory over Goliath, the text says "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit, like two threads. Then Jonathan does something startling. He takes off his own robe and gives it to David, with his sword, his bow and his belt. Some readers see a prince handing over the signs of his rank. Then the friendship gets expensive. Saul turns on David and wants him dead, and Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. He warns David, at real risk to himself. Later, the text has him say it outright: you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. The heir steps aside in his own words. Readers have heard this bond in more than one way, and the text itself calls it love and a covenant. Then comes what David did after the grief. After the lament, after David becomes king, he asks a question nobody needed him to ask: "Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" There is: Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, living quietly far from court. David sends for him, gives him back his grandfather's land, and seats him at the king's table for good. Kindness here is that same Hebrew word from yesterday, chesed. The friend is gone. The friendship keeps going, now as a seat at the table for his son.
screen: `TWO SOULS KNIT TOGETHER.` · `A PRINCE GIVES AWAY HIS ROBE.` · `CAUGHT BETWEEN FATHER AND FRIEND.` · `A SEAT AT THE TABLE FOR HIS SON.` · then, large: `FOR JONATHAN'S SAKE.`

segments.voice: Let an old friend come to mind. Someone who once stood next to you, at school, at work, in a hard year, and whom life has carried somewhere else. Breathe, and remember one specific thing: a joke, a kitchen, a drive, something they did for you. Hold it for a few breaths. Then let a first sentence of a note form in your head. Not an apology for the silence. Just the memory, and that you thought of them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
David and Jonathan. A king's son and the man who would take his father's throne, knit together as friends, with a kindness that outlived Jonathan. Today's word.
Your line: the friend. Today, write to that old friend, even three lines, and send it. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

829.title: Strong as death
829.howItsDone: Some Jewish communities read the Song of Songs in the synagogue during Passover, and lines from its eighth chapter are read at some weddings, Jewish and Christian.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David and Jonathan, and a kindness that outlived a friend. Your line was the friend. Did those three lines to an old friend get sent? Today, a love poem from the Bible. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

A seal is a small thing. A carved stone or a ring, pressed into wax or clay, and the mark it leaves says: this is mine, this comes from me. Near the end of the Song of Songs, one lover asks to become one. Not to be given one, or to wear one. To be the seal, pressed onto the other's heart and arm. And then, in the same breath, the poem makes a bold claim about love. It doesn't say love is sweet, or kind, or patient. It picks a much bigger rival. Today: love that is strong as death.
screen: `A SEAL: THIS IS MINE.` → `PRESSED ONTO THE HEART.` → `A MUCH BIGGER RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse in the King James: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death." First, the seal. The speaker doesn't ask to be remembered fondly. She asks to be the mark itself, on the heart where feeling lives and on the arm where work gets done. Love here is meant to show, inside and out. Second, the comparison. Death is a force nobody bargains with, and it doesn't let go. The poem says love is like that: just as strong, just as unwilling to let go. The next line is harder: "jealousy is cruel as the grave." The poem doesn't pretend love is only gentle. It's fierce, and it burns: the text calls its coals "coals of fire." Third, the water. The following verse adds: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." Floods of water, and love is the fire they can't put out. Fourth, how it's read. Read plainly, the Song is love poetry between two lovers, and some readers take it that way. Jewish tradition has also read it as the love between God and Israel; the Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva calling the Song the holy of holies among the scriptures. Christian readers have heard Christ and the church, or God and the soul. These readings sit side by side, and the poem holds all of them. Whichever you hear, the claim is the same, and it's bold: love isn't the soft thing in the room. It's as strong as death.
screen: `SET ME AS A SEAL.` · `STRONG AS DEATH, CRUEL AS THE GRAVE.` · `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH IT.` · `LOVERS, GOD AND ISRAEL, OR THE SOUL.` · then, large: `LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Who do you love and rarely tell? A partner, a parent, a child, a friend. Breathe, and choose one, and let their face come. Now find one sentence you have been too shy, too busy or too cool to say. Not a hint. The plain thing. I love you. I'm proud of you. You changed my life. Say it silently a few times, slowly, until it feels less strange. If you pray, let that sentence become a prayer for them. The bell holds the time.
Strong as death. The Song of Songs' claim that love holds on as hard as death does, and that many waters cannot quench it. Today's word.
Your line: strong as death. Today, say that sentence out loud to the person you chose, without softening it into a joke. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: God is love
830.hook: a short letter answers what God is in three words
830.howItsDone: Christians read First John in worship and private prayer, and the line God is love appears on church walls, cards and gravestones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs: love set like a seal. Your line was strong as death. Did that plain sentence get said out loud? Today, from the Hebrew Bible to the New Testament, and a three-word sentence. Day eight hundred thirty.

Ask a room of people what God is, and the answers get long fast. Maker of everything. Judge. Spirit. Mystery. Philosophers keep trying. Near the end of the New Testament there's a short letter, traditionally linked to the apostle John, that answers in three words. Not God has love, or God gives love, or God loves. Something stranger, and harder to get out of: God is love. Today, that sentence, and the test the same letter attaches to it.
screen: `WHAT IS GOD?` → `THE ANSWERS GET LONG.` → `A LETTER ANSWERS IN THREE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the King James, in the fourth chapter of First John: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." First, notice the shape. The letter doesn't say love is one of God's qualities, the way we'd say a person is tall or patient. It says God is love, as if love were what God is made of. Christian writers keep turning that over. Second, notice the problem the letter raises a few verses later: "No man hath seen God at any time." So how would anyone know God? The letter's answer: "If we love one another, God dwelleth in us." The unseen God shows up where people love each other. Third, the order. "We love him, because he first loved us." In this letter love doesn't start with us. It's received first, then passed on. Fourth, the test, and it's blunt. "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar." The letter's reasoning is simple: if you can't love the brother you can see, how would you love God, whom you can't? So the sentence God is love isn't only a comfort. It's a measuring stick. Whatever else a reader believes about God, in this letter the sentence asks for something practical. In the letter's terms, love isn't proven in the sky. It's proven at the kitchen table, the office, the group chat, with the person right in front of you.
screen: `NOT GOD LOVES: GOD IS LOVE.` · `NO MAN HATH SEEN GOD.` · `WE LOVE, BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED.` · `THE TEST: THE BROTHER YOU CAN SEE.` · then, large: `GOD IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let one ordinary moment of today come to mind, something still ahead of you: a meeting, a meal, a drive, a conversation that usually goes sideways. Picture the person you'll see there. Now ask: what would it look like to act from love in that moment, just once? Not a feeling to force. An act. Listening to the end. Letting them go first. Saying thank you and meaning it. If you pray, you can rest in those three words from First John. If not, just rest with the person's face. The bell holds the time.
God is love. First John's three-word answer to what God is, with a test attached: love the brother you can see. Today's word.
Your line: god is love. Today, in the moment you pictured, do the one loving act you chose, and notice what changes. Day eight hundred thirty.

831.title: Love your enemies
831.hook: love your enemies, pray for them that persecute you
831.howItsDone: Christians pray for people they find difficult, sometimes by name in private prayer, and some churches include prayers for enemies or for those who wish them harm in their regular worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three words from First John. Your line was god is love. Did you get to act from love in the moment you pictured? Today, the hardest test of that sentence. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

Loving a friend is easy to admire. Loving a stranger, as we heard a few days ago, takes some work. But there is often someone in a life who is neither: the coworker who undermined you, the relative who keeps score, the ex, the neighbor with the leaf blower and the grudge. On a mountain in Galilee, in the teaching Christians call the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus names that person directly. And he doesn't say tolerate them, or avoid them, or forgive them eventually. He says something that sounds almost impossible. Today: even them.
screen: `A FRIEND, A STRANGER.` → `AND THE PERSON WHO HURT YOU.` → `A SERMON ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The King James puts it like this: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." And the verse goes on: pray for those who mistreat and persecute you. First, notice the verbs. Love, bless, do good, pray. None of them is a feeling you have to fake. Each one is something a person can do, even while the hurt is still there. Second, the reason Jesus gives. God, he says, "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." The sunrise doesn't check anyone's record. Neither does the rain. To love an enemy, in this teaching, is to be a little like the weather God sends: given to everyone. Third, the roots. This isn't a break with the scripture Jesus grew up with. The book of Proverbs already says, "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat." Jesus takes up that thread and carries it on, from bread to blessing to prayer. Fourth, the Gospels show him doing it. In Luke, from the cross, he prays for the men crucifying him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Christians apply this teaching in different ways. Some traditions, like the Mennonites and the Quakers, read it as a call to refuse violence altogether. Other churches read it as a command about the heart and daily conduct that still leaves room for defending the innocent. Both sides take the command seriously. Love here isn't approval. It's wanting good for someone who doesn't want good for you.
screen: `LOVE, BLESS, DO GOOD, PRAY.` · `SUN ON THE EVIL AND ON THE GOOD.` · `IF THINE ENEMY BE HUNGRY.` · `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Let one difficult person come to mind. Not the worst one. Someone who is hard, but whom you can picture without your stomach knotting completely. Breathe. Notice what rises: anger, hurt, tiredness. Let it be there. Now, slowly, wish them one ordinary good thing. Sleep tonight. A day without pain. Someone who is kind to them. You don't have to mean it perfectly. Just send it. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Love your enemies. Jesus's teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: love, bless, do good and pray for those who hurt you, as the sun rises on everyone. Today's word.
Your line: even them. Today, when that person crosses your mind, wish them one good thing before you go back to being annoyed. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: Washing feet
832.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and some other churches hold a foot-washing on the Thursday before Easter, and some smaller churches wash one another's feet as part of communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sermon on the Mount: love your enemies. Your line was even them. Did you manage to wish that difficult person one good thing? Today, love you can see, and smell, and get wet from. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

A towel, a basin, some water. That's the whole scene's equipment. It's the last supper Jesus shares with his friends before his arrest, in John's Gospel, and the room is full of people who have walked dusty roads in sandals. Partway through the meal, he gets up. He takes off his outer garment, ties the towel around his waist, pours water into the basin, and kneels in front of the first pair of feet. The room goes quiet. One of them is about to object, loudly. Today: washing feet.
screen: `A TOWEL, A BASIN, SOME WATER.` → `HE GETS UP FROM SUPPER.` → `HE KNEELS AT THEIR FEET.`

segments.voice: John opens the scene with one sentence about love: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then, instead of a speech, a chore. First, whose job this was. When Abigail agrees to marry David in First Samuel, she says, "let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." In her words, washing feet is the task of a servant who serves the servants. Second, Peter. He can't stand it. "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, being Peter, swings all the way the other way: then not just my feet, but my hands and my head. Letting yourself be served turns out to be its own kind of humility. Third, who gets washed. The text says Jesus knew who would betray him, and readers notice that no one is skipped. Judas's feet were in that room too. Fourth, the instruction. When he sits back down, he says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." And: "I have given you an example." Churches take that in different ways. Some churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican among them, wash feet in a service on the Thursday before Easter. Some smaller churches wash feet together whenever they share communion. Others read it as a picture of everyday service rather than a rite. The gesture at the center stays the same: love that kneels down.
screen: `A SERVANT'S JOB.` · `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.` · `NO ONE IS SKIPPED.` · `I HAVE GIVEN YOU AN EXAMPLE.` · then, large: `WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look down at your own feet for a moment. Then let a person come to mind whom you could serve today in a small, low, unglamorous way. Not a grand gesture. The dishes no one wants. Taking out their trash. Carrying the heavy bag. Covering the boring shift. Picture yourself doing it without announcing it. Then notice: is there someone you've refused to let serve you? If you pray, you can bring both to God in a few plain words. The bell holds the time.
Washing feet. In John's Gospel, Jesus takes a servant's job at his last supper and tells his friends to do the same for one another. Today's word.
Your line: wash feet. Today, do the low job you pictured for someone, quietly, and don't mention it. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

833.title: No greater love
833.hook: greater love hath no man than this, that he lay down his life for his friends
833.howItsDone: Christian tradition reads John 15:13 as Jesus describing his own death, and the verse is read at some funerals and carved on some memorials to people who died for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a towel and a basin. Your line was wash feet. Did you do the low job quietly, without mentioning it? Today, the same night, a little later, and the week's last day. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

The feet are washed. The basin is put away. In John's Gospel, Jesus keeps talking to his friends late into that last evening, and it reads like someone saying everything that matters before a door closes. Somewhere in that long talk comes one sentence about love. It sets a bar, and it's high. And then, in the next breath, it changes what the friends are called. Today: no greater love.
screen: `THE BASIN IS PUT AWAY.` → `A LONG TALK BEFORE A DOOR CLOSES.` → `ONE SENTENCE SETS THE BAR.`

segments.voice: First, the command it explains. Just before, Jesus says: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you." Not as much as you can manage. As I have loved you. Second, the sentence itself: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." In John's story it is said the night before the crucifixion, and Christian tradition hears it pointing straight at the next day: he is describing what he is about to do. Third, the word friends. A moment later he says, "Henceforth I call you not servants" but "I have called you friends." The Greek word is a form of philos, the friend-love from earlier this block. The same men whose feet he washed like a servant, he now calls friends. The rank goes the other way from what the room expected. Fourth, the small version. Dying for a friend is not a request that comes to everyone. Some readers also hear a quieter meaning: a life can be laid down an hour at a time. A night shift at a sickbed. A weekend given up. A plan let go so a friend can have theirs. And a look back at the week of love's voices: where you go, the friend, strong as death, god is love, even them, wash feet, and now lay it down. Ruth stayed, Jonathan stepped aside, the Song set love against death, John made it the test, and Jesus took the towel and named the bar.

segments.voice: Choose one friend who could use something from you this week. Breathe, and look at what you were planning to keep for yourself: an evening, a little money, the last word in an argument, the front seat, the favor you've been saving. Pick one small thing you could set down for them. Hold the picture of handing it over, and notice the little cost. That cost is the point. If you pray, you can offer it with their name. The bell holds the time.
No greater love. Jesus's words in John's Gospel: laying down your life for your friends, said the night before he died, and lived in smaller ways an hour at a time. Today's word.
Your line: lay it down. Today, give up the one thing you chose for your friend, and let it cost you a little. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

what it means: Jesus, the night before he dies, naming the highest love as giving your life for your friends, then calling his disciples friends.
what a scholar hears: the Greek for life here is psyche, also soul, and friends is philoi: the servants of the foot-washing become friends.
